note: Short tax facts, one sentence each, with a source. One is shown each day.

items.text: The 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $24,150 for heads of household, and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly.
In 2026, people 65 or older (or blind) add $2,050 to the standard deduction if unmarried, or $1,650 each if married.
For 2026, the 37% top federal rate applies to taxable income over $640,600 for single filers and $768,700 for joint filers.
For 2026, a single filer pays 10% federal tax on the first $12,400 of taxable income.
Federal brackets are progressive: moving into a higher bracket only raises the rate on the dollars above that bracket’s starting point.
Long-term capital gains can be taxed at 0%: for 2026, that covers taxable income up to $49,450 for single filers and $98,900 for joint filers.
For 2026, long-term capital gains above $545,500 of taxable income for single filers ($613,700 joint) are taxed at 20%.
Ohio taxes 2026 nonbusiness income above $26,050 at a flat 2.75% rate.
The 2026 Social Security wage base is $184,500. Wages above that aren’t subject to the 6.2% Social Security tax.
Medicare tax of 1.45% applies to all wages, with no cap.
An extra 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to wages over $200,000 for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.
The 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax can apply to investment income for people with modified AGI over $200,000 ($250,000 joint).
The 2026 annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per recipient.
The 2026 federal estate tax basic exclusion amount is $15 million per person.
The 2026 foreign earned income exclusion is $132,900.
The 2026 limit for health flexible spending account contributions is $3,400.
Employers can provide up to $340 a month in tax-free transit or parking benefits in 2026.
The Child Tax Credit is worth up to $2,200 per qualifying child for 2026, with up to $1,700 of it refundable.
The maximum 2026 Earned Income Tax Credit is $8,231 for families with three or more qualifying children.
Workers without qualifying children can claim the EITC too: the 2026 maximum is $664.
You can’t claim the 2026 EITC if your investment income is over $12,200.
A tax credit cuts your tax dollar for dollar; a deduction only lowers the income your tax is figured on.
A refundable credit can give you a refund even if you owe no tax.
The 2026 adoption credit is up to $17,670 per child, and up to $5,120 of it can be refundable.
The American Opportunity Tax Credit is worth up to $2,500 per eligible student, and up to $1,000 of it is refundable.
The Lifetime Learning Credit is worth up to $2,000 per tax return.
You may be able to deduct up to $2,500 of student loan interest a year.
Starting with 2026, the child and dependent care credit can cover up to 50% of qualifying expenses for lower-income families.
From 2025 through 2028, people 65 and older may deduct an extra $6,000 each, on top of the regular senior standard deduction, with a phase-out above $75,000 of income ($150,000 joint).

items.text: From 2025 through 2028, workers may deduct up to $25,000 a year of qualified tips.

sources.title: IRS: Working Families Tax Cuts, individuals and workers

items.text: From 2025 through 2028, workers may deduct up to $12,500 of qualified overtime pay ($25,000 for joint filers), with a phase-out above $150,000 of income ($300,000 joint).

sources.title: IRS: Working Families Tax Cuts, individuals and workers

items.text: From 2025 through 2028, interest on a loan for a qualifying new personal vehicle may be deductible, up to $10,000 a year.

sources.title: IRS: Working Families Tax Cuts, individuals and workers

items.text: Starting with 2026, people who don’t itemize may deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts to qualified charities ($2,000 for joint filers).
Trump Accounts for children began accepting contributions on July 4, 2026, with a one-time $1,000 federal contribution for each eligible child.
You can put up to $24,500 into a 401(k) in 2026, plus up to $8,000 more if you’re 50 or older.
People aged 60 through 63 get a larger 2026 401(k) catch-up limit: $11,250.
The 2026 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, or $8,600 if you’re 50 or older.
You can make IRA contributions for a tax year up until that year’s filing deadline, usually April 15.
Required minimum distributions generally start at age 73, or age 75 for people born in 1960 or later.
Roth IRAs don’t require minimum distributions while the original owner is alive.
Taking money out of a retirement plan before age 59½ can add a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies.
Up to 85% of Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax, depending on your other income.
The 2026 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment is 2.8%.
A SIMPLE IRA allows up to $17,000 of employee contributions in 2026.
Filing electronically with direct deposit is the fastest way to get a refund.
The IRS issues most refunds for e-filed returns in less than 21 days.
An extension gives you more time to file, but not more time to pay. Tax owed is still due by the April deadline.
Form 4868 gives individuals an automatic six-month extension to file.
To claim a refund, you generally must file within three years of the return’s due date.

sources.title: IRS: Filing past due tax returns

items.text: Head of household status gives a bigger standard deduction than single status: $24,150 vs. $16,100 for 2026.
Married couples filing jointly are both responsible for the tax on the return, even if only one had income.
Form 1040-X is used to fix a return you’ve already filed.
If you move, Form 8822 tells the IRS your new address so letters reach you.
Employers must give workers their W-2 by January 31 (or the next business day).
The IRS often postpones deadlines for people in federally declared disaster areas.
The failure-to-file penalty is generally 5% of unpaid tax for each month a return is late, up to 25%.
The failure-to-pay penalty is generally 0.5% of unpaid tax per month, up to 25%.
Filing on time even when you can’t pay avoids the larger failure-to-file penalty.
If you can’t pay in full, the IRS offers payment plans, and many can be set up online.
You may owe an estimated tax penalty if you didn’t pay enough during the year through withholding or estimated payments.
Self-employment tax is 15.3%: 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare.
You generally owe self-employment tax if your net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more.
Half of your self-employment tax is deductible when you figure your adjusted gross income.
Estimated tax payments are usually due April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.
The simplified home office deduction is $5 per square foot of qualifying space, up to 300 square feet.
The business standard mileage rate was 72.5 cents a mile for January through June 2026 and 76 cents from July 1, 2026.
Commuting between your home and your regular workplace isn’t deductible as a business expense.
Business meals are generally only 50% deductible.
Payments to contractors made after 2025 must be reported on Form 1099-NEC once they reach $2,000 for the year.
Bartering is taxable: the fair market value of goods or services you receive counts as income.
Employment tax records should be kept at least four years.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.text: Gambling winnings are taxable income, and some gambling losses may be deductible if you itemize.
Unemployment compensation is taxable on your federal return.
Tips are income. Employees must report tips of $20 or more in a month to their employer.
Alimony under divorce or separation agreements made after 2018 isn’t deductible by the payer or taxable to the recipient.
Selling digital assets such as cryptocurrency can be a taxable event, and Form 1040 asks about digital asset activity.
Up to $3,000 of net capital losses a year ($1,500 if married filing separately) can offset other income; the rest carries forward.
An investment held more than one year produces a long-term gain or loss; one year or less is short-term.
If you meet the ownership and use tests, you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on selling your home ($500,000 for most married couples filing jointly).
In most cases, keep tax records for three years after you file.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.text: Keep records about property, such as a home or investments, until the time to amend expires for the year you sell it.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.text: An IRS tax transcript can show your past return information if you’ve lost a copy.
The IRS usually contacts people first by regular mail, not by phone, email, text, or social media.

sources.title: IRS: How to know it’s really the IRS

items.text: The IRS won’t demand immediate payment by gift card, prepaid debit card, or wire transfer.

sources.title: IRS: How to know it’s really the IRS

items.text: An Identity Protection PIN is a six-digit number that helps stop someone from filing a tax return with your Social Security number.

sources.title: IRS: Get an Identity Protection PIN

items.text: Anyone with an SSN or ITIN who can verify their identity can get an IRS Identity Protection PIN.

sources.title: IRS: Get an Identity Protection PIN

items.text: The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent office inside the IRS that helps people whose tax problems aren’t being resolved.
Every taxpayer has ten rights under the Taxpayer Bill of Rights, including the right to be informed and the right to appeal.
The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator can help you fill out a new W-4 so you don’t owe a lot or over-withhold.
A very large refund usually means too much was withheld from your pay during the year.
Bonuses are often withheld at a flat 22% federal rate, but they’re taxed like other wages when you file.
Your filing status generally depends on whether you’re married on the last day of the year.
There are five filing statuses: single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, and qualifying surviving spouse.
If more than one filing status applies to you, you can generally choose the one that gives you the lowest tax.
A qualifying surviving spouse can use joint-return tax rates for up to two years after a spouse’s death if they have a dependent child.
Whether you must file a return depends on your filing status, age, and gross income.
Even if you aren’t required to file, filing may be worth it to get back withholding or claim refundable credits.
Dependents can be either a qualifying child or a qualifying relative, and each has its own tests.
A dependent’s own standard deduction is limited, but it’s at least $1,350 for 2026.
Most taxpayers take the standard deduction because it’s larger than their itemized deductions.
You can itemize or take the standard deduction, whichever is larger, but not both.
If you’re married filing separately and your spouse itemizes, you must itemize too.
You can choose to have your refund split across more than one bank account.
The IRS Where’s My Refund? tool updates once a day, usually overnight.
IRS Free File lets eligible taxpayers prepare and file their federal return online at no cost.
Publication 17 is the IRS’s main guide to filing an individual federal return.
Publication 509 lists the year’s federal tax deadlines for individuals, businesses, and employers.
If a tax deadline falls on a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day.
An amended return generally must be filed within three years of the original return or two years of paying the tax, whichever is later, to get a refund.
You can view your federal balance, payment history, and transcripts in your IRS Online Account.
If you can’t file on time, filing for an extension avoids the failure-to-file penalty, but interest still runs on unpaid tax.
Interest from bank accounts is generally taxable, even if you don’t receive a Form 1099-INT.
Interest on most state and local government bonds is exempt from federal income tax, but still has to be reported.
Qualified dividends are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates.
Scholarships used for tuition and required fees are generally tax-free; amounts used for room and board are generally taxable.
Social Security benefits are reported to you each year on Form SSA-1099.
Income from a side business is taxable even if it’s small and even if you don’t get a 1099.
Money you get from selling personal items for less than you paid generally isn’t taxable, but a gain on a sale is.
Rental income is taxable, and you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses of renting the property.
If you rent out a home for fewer than 15 days during the year and use it as a home, the rent generally isn’t taxable.
Depreciation lets rental property owners deduct the cost of the building (not the land) over time.
Gambling winnings must be reported even if you don’t receive a Form W-2G.
Prizes and awards, including the value of non-cash prizes, are generally taxable.
Cash, gift cards, and gifts of property you receive aren’t taxable income to you, though the giver may need to file a gift tax return.
If you sell your main home and qualify for the exclusion, you may not need to report the sale unless you received a Form 1099-S.
To use the home sale exclusion, you generally must have owned and lived in the home for at least two of the five years before the sale.
Losses on the sale of your personal home or personal belongings aren’t deductible.
Your basis in an investment usually includes what you paid plus commissions and fees.
Inherited property generally gets a basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death.
Digital assets received as payment for goods or services are taxable at their fair market value when received.
The child and dependent care credit applies to care for children under 13 or a spouse or dependent who can’t care for themselves.
For the child and dependent care credit, qualifying expenses are capped at $3,000 for one person and $6,000 for two or more.
Day camp can count toward the child and dependent care credit, but overnight camp doesn’t.
To claim the child care credit you must report the care provider’s name, address, and taxpayer ID number.
The American Opportunity Tax Credit can be claimed for the first four years of higher education.
The Lifetime Learning Credit has no limit on the number of years you can claim it, and it covers courses to improve job skills.
Form 1098-T from the school helps you figure education credits, but the credit is based on what you actually paid.
Eligible educators can deduct some unreimbursed classroom expenses even if they don’t itemize.
The Earned Income Tax Credit is refundable, so it can produce a refund even if you owe no tax.
To claim the EITC, you need earned income, and you, your spouse, and any qualifying children generally need valid Social Security numbers.
By law, the IRS can’t issue refunds that include the EITC or the Additional Child Tax Credit before mid-February.
A qualifying child for the Child Tax Credit must be under age 17 at the end of the year.
The $500 credit for other dependents can apply to older children and other relatives who don’t qualify for the Child Tax Credit.
The home mortgage interest deduction is available only if you itemize.
Medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, and only if you itemize.
For any single charitable gift of $250 or more, you need a written acknowledgment from the charity.
Gifts to individuals, even people in need, aren’t deductible as charitable contributions.
The value of your time volunteering isn’t deductible, but some out-of-pocket volunteer costs can be.
You can deduct student loan interest even if you don’t itemize, subject to income limits.
Contributions to a traditional IRA may be deductible, depending on your income and whether you’re covered by a workplace plan.
Health Savings Account contributions can lower your taxable income, and qualified withdrawals for medical costs are tax-free.
Roth IRA contributions aren’t deductible, but qualified withdrawals, including earnings, are tax-free.
You can contribute to a Roth IRA only if your income is below certain limits.
A spouse with little or no income may still be able to contribute to an IRA based on the working spouse’s income.
Rolling over a retirement distribution within 60 days generally avoids tax on it.
A direct rollover between retirement accounts avoids the mandatory 20% withholding that applies to some plan distributions paid to you.
Your first required minimum distribution can wait until April 1 of the year after you reach the required age, but then two are due that year.
Exceptions to the 10% early distribution tax include certain disability, medical expense, and separation-from-service situations.
The age 60 to 63 “super catch-up” for workplace plans was created by the SECURE 2.0 Act.
Workplace retirement contributions generally must come out of a paycheck by December 31 to count for that year.
If Social Security is your only income, your benefits generally aren’t taxable.
You can ask to have federal tax withheld from Social Security benefits using Form W-4V.
A sole proprietor reports business income and expenses on Schedule C with their individual return.
A business expense must be both ordinary and necessary to be deductible.
Startup costs can be partly deducted in the first year and the rest spread over 15 years.
An Employer Identification Number (EIN) is free to get directly from the IRS.
You generally need an EIN if you have employees, operate as a corporation or partnership, or file certain excise or employment tax returns.
Whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor depends on the control the business has over the work, not just the job title.
Employers must withhold income tax and the employee share of Social Security and Medicare from wages, and pay a matching employer share.
Employers report wages and withholding to the IRS quarterly on Form 941.
Federal unemployment tax (FUTA) is paid only by employers, not withheld from employees’ wages.
The home office deduction requires space used regularly and exclusively for business.
You can use either the standard mileage rate or actual car expenses, but rules limit switching methods.
Business gifts are deductible only up to $25 per recipient per year.
Travel expenses are deductible when you’re away from your tax home overnight for business.
The qualified business income deduction can be up to 20% of qualified business income for many pass-through business owners.
Starting in 2026, the qualified business income deduction has a minimum of $400 for taxpayers with at least $1,000 of qualified business income.
Payments by credit card or payment app may be reported to you on Form 1099-K.
If you close a business, you generally need to file final returns and mark them as final.
Keep records that support your business income and deductions for as long as they may be needed for the tax law.
IRS interest on unpaid tax is figured daily, so paying sooner reduces what you owe.
If a return is more than 60 days late, a minimum failure-to-file penalty applies.
First-time penalty relief may be available if you have a clean history with the IRS.
Setting up a payment plan can reduce the failure-to-pay penalty rate while the plan is in effect.
The estimated tax penalty may be waived if the underpayment was due to a casualty, disaster, or other unusual circumstance.
You can pay the IRS directly from a bank account for free using IRS Direct Pay.
Tax preparers must sign returns and include their Preparer Tax Identification Number.

sources.title: IRS: Recognize tax scams and fraud

items.text: Never sign a blank tax return or one you haven’t reviewed: you’re responsible for what’s on it.

sources.title: IRS: Recognize tax scams and fraud

items.text: If you receive an IRS letter, compare it with your return carefully; many issues can be resolved by mail.
You have the right to appeal most IRS decisions to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals.
Help from the Taxpayer Advocate Service is free.
The IRS doesn’t call to demand payment without first sending a bill by mail.

sources.title: IRS: How to know it’s really the IRS

items.text: Be wary of “ghost preparers” who won’t sign the return they prepared.

sources.title: IRS: Recognize tax scams and fraud

items.text: Scammers often promise a large refund for a fee; the IRS warns against anyone who bases fees on the size of your refund.

sources.title: IRS: Recognize tax scams and fraud

items.text: You can change your W-4 at any time during the year.
If both spouses work, completing the W-4 Step 2 helps avoid under-withholding.
Withholding is treated as paid evenly through the year, which can help cover a shortfall late in the year.
You can have federal tax withheld from unemployment benefits by filing Form W-4V.
Gambling winnings over certain amounts may have federal tax withheld at 24%.
Keep copies of your filed tax returns; they help when preparing future returns and amending past ones.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.text: If you lose a W-2, contact your employer first; if that doesn’t work, the IRS can help.
Records of home improvements help reduce the taxable gain when you sell your home.
Electronic records are acceptable to the IRS if they’re accurate and readable.
